scenario: gym corporate membership for an office of 40

seller.product: Corporate wellness membership (4 centres, group classes, monthly trainer assessment)
price_list: Corporate annual plan ₹1,800 per head per month, minimum 25 heads, 12-month term
Pay-per-visit ₹180 per visit, minimum billing ₹30,000 per month
3-month pilot: 20 heads at ₹1,600 per head per month, no lock-in

speakers.name: Tanvi Malhotra
speakers.style: corporate partnerships executive, upbeat, persistent, quick with options, sometimes pitches past what she hears

speakers.name: Sudhir Nair
speakers.style: HR head of Quillstone Analytics, sceptical, burned by a past tie-up, very direct about money

speakers.name: Ankita Joshi
speakers.style: HR executive for employee engagement, practical, knows shift patterns and staff requests

coaching_truths.statement: On the low-uptake story from the previous gym she asked why people stopped going, then answered with a monthly usage report and a pay-per-visit model.
She claimed PulseHub had no proper showers or lockers; the prospect had visited himself and contradicted her, and she had to take it back.
Ankita said half the women had asked for a gym last month; Tanvi went on listing classes instead of building the pilot around that demand.
The HR head said the office moves to a new tower in January, which changes the nearest centre; Tanvi skipped past it to pricing.
Asked to match the competitor price, she refused honestly and offered a no-lock-in pilot that removed the risk instead of cutting the annual price.
She misstated the weekday opening time as 5:30 and corrected it to 6 a.m. in the middle of a timing objection, which costs credibility.
